Missing one repeated copy creates inconsistent answers. This is an update anomaly.
Separate the author entity from the notes that refer to it. Store the name once under an author ID.

DISTINCT removes repeated identical result rows. The fixture guarantees one name per ID; conflicting source names would require a separate resolution policy.

after: If every note stores its author's name, changing that name means editing many copies. The project starts with `raw_notes(note_id, author_id, author_name, title)`.
If one copy is missed, different rows disagree about the same author. This problem is called an update anomaly.
Store each author's name once in an authors table, using the author's ID.
Keep author_id in each note. A join can bring back the author's name when you need to display it.
Two people can share a name. Use their supplied author IDs to keep them separate.
DISTINCT removes identical pairs. It does not decide which name is right if one ID has two different names. The project data has one consistent name for each ID.
Create authors from the distinct author ID/name pairs. Copy every raw note into notes, keeping its note ID, author ID, and title. Keep raw_notes unchanged.
This organization is called normalization. It groups facts by what they describe. It does not mean putting every column in a separate table.

before.question: Two authors are both named Sam, with IDs 10 and 20. Why should a notes table store author_id rather than use name as its identity?
choices: IDs preserve which Sam wrote each note despite matching names.
A foreign key automatically changes the authors’ names.
before.explanation: A display name can be shared or changed. The stable key keeps the relationship attached to the intended author.

after.question: Two authors named Sam have IDs 10 and 20. Why should notes store author_id?
choices: The IDs keep each note connected to the right Sam.
A foreign key changes both authors' names.
after.explanation: Names can match or change. The ID keeps the note connected to the intended author.
